features.claim: It had two parallel rows of tall spines down its neck and back.
features.quote: Most distinctively, it sported two parallel rows of tall spines down its neck and back, taller than in any other known sauropod.

features.claim: The spines on its neck were incredibly long.
features.quote: The spines on its neck vertebrae were incredibly long.

features.claim: It had a long tail and neck, a small head, and a barrel-shaped trunk held up by four column-like legs.
features.quote: It followed the typical sauropod body plan, with a long tail and neck, a small head, and a barrel-shaped trunk supported by four column-like legs.

features.claim: Its neck was shorter than in most other sauropods.
features.quote: The neck of Amargasaurus was shorter than in most other sauropods, a common trait within the Dicraeosauridae.

features.claim: Its front legs were a little shorter than its back legs.
features.quote: The forelimbs were somewhat shorter than the hind limbs, as in related sauropods.
Amargasaurus was quadrupedal (moved on four legs), and probably was unable to rear on its hind legs.

features.claim: It had a long, low skull on the end of a long neck.
features.quote: It was a quadrupedal herbivore with a long, low skull on the end of a long neck, much like its relative Dicraeosaurus.

features.claim: It was small for a sauropod, about 9 to 13 meters long.
features.quote: Amargasaurus was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 13 meters (30 to 43 feet) in length and weighing approximately 2.5–4 metric tons (2.8–4.4 short tons).

features.claim: The spines on the middle of its neck were the tallest.
features.quote: The tallest spines could be found on the middle part of the neck, where they reached 60 centimeters (24 inches) on the 8th cervical.

features.claim: On the neck the spines were bowed backward, sticking up above the vertebra next to them.
features.quote: On the neck, they were bowed backward, projecting above the adjacent vertebra.

features.claim: The spines on the last two back vertebrae, the hip and the front of the tail were not split in two but flared into a paddle-shaped upper end.
features.quote: The last two dorsal vertebrae, the hip, and the foremost tail in Amargasaurus also had elongated spines; these were not bifurcated but flared into a paddle-shaped upper end.

not_this.claim: Old pictures showing the spines covered by a horn sheath are wrong; the spines did not support a keratinous sheath.
not_this.quote: In 2022, a study by Ignacio Cerda and colleagues analyzing the external and internal bone structure of the spines of Amargasaurus and an indeterminate dicraeosaurid (also from the La Amarga Formation) suggested that the spines did not support a keratinous sheath as previously believed.

not_this.claim: Old pictures showing the head held nearly horizontal are wrong, because that posture would have been anatomically impossible.
not_this.quote: The first skeletal reconstructions show the skull in a near-horizontal posture. Salgado, in 1999, argued that such a posture would have been anatomically impossible due to the elongated neural spines of the neck vertebrae.

not_this.claim: The idea that it had two parallel skin sails is unlikely, because the space between the two rows of spines was only 3 to 7 cm.
not_this.quote: As the space between both rows was merely 3 to 7 cm (1.2 to 2.8 inches), the existence of two parallel sails seems unlikely.

not_this.claim: The idea that neck sails would have reduced neck flexion is a reason the two-sail picture is unlikely.
not_this.quote: Gregory Paul, in 1994, considered this possibility unlikely, noting that neck sails would have reduced neck flexion, and that the spines were circular in cross-section rather than flattened as is the case in sail-bearing animals.

debated.claim: What the tall spines were for is not known.
debated.quote: Both the function and the appearance in life of the extremely elongated and bifurcated vertebral spines remain elusive.

debated.claim: One idea is that the spines supported a sail-like structure.
debated.quote: Another idea is that they supported a sail-like structure.

debated.claim: One idea is that the spines were connected by ligaments and could have formed a scaffold supporting a neck sail.
debated.quote: Analysis of the bone structure suggests that the spines were connected by ligaments and could have formed a scaffold supporting a neck sail.

second_reading.quote: A herbivore, it shared its environment with at least three other sauropod genera, which might have exploited different food sources in order to reduce competition.
